title: Diwali Gifting 2026: Handcrafted Finds From Indian Design Studios
excerpt: Blue-pottery diyas, illustrated terracotta and Pichwai-inspired hampers: this year's Diwali gifts are handmade, design-led and built to outlast the festival.
body:
• Diwali 2026 gifting is shifting from standard sweet boxes to handcrafted pieces from Indian studios — blue pottery, terracotta, resin and heritage craft.
  • Women-led labels lead the diya edit: Ekatra Handmade's Rajasthani blue-pottery sets, Happy Earth Studio's illustrated terracotta, and Gulmeher's soy-wax diyas made by women waste-pickers turned artisans.
  • Budgets span widely: design-led hampers run from about Rs 18,500 for The Leela's Opulence Hamper to Rs 50,000 for Conrad Bengaluru's Heart of Delight.
  • Order early and choose pieces that outlast the festival — diyas, urlis and tableware that return for every puja and family dinner.

The most wanted Diwali gifts of 2026 are not coming off a factory line. Across Indian design studios and women-led craft labels, the festival's familiar objects — the diya above all — are being remade by hand in blue pottery, illustrated terracotta, resin and recycled materials, and buyers are choosing them over the standard box of sweets.

The diya, remade seven ways

Women Listed's Diya Edit rounds up seven women-led labels giving the festive lamp a distinct identity. Ekatra Handmade, founded in Kota by mother-daughter duo Minakshi and Aishwarya Jhawar, finishes its diya sets in the cobalt-and-white language of Rajasthani blue pottery and builds them into hampers and corporate gifts. Jalna's Happy Earth Studio treats terracotta as a canvas, hand-painting tea-light holders with regional characters such as its Raja-Rani couples. Mumbai's Crafty Shea works at the decorative end — resin diyas and tea-light holders designed to hold a dressed table before they are ever lit.

Heritage and livelihood run through the rest of the edit. Gharana, a craft house with roots in a 1945 Himachal Pradesh workshop, sells hand-painted clay diyas on their own or inside branded corporate hampers. East Delhi's Gulmeher Foundation makes soy-wax diyas and festive boxes while creating skilled livelihoods for women from vulnerable communities, including former waste-pickers. Bengaluru's Diya Innovations produces hand-painted diyas and curated festive boxes through an inclusive model that employs adults with intellectual disabilities, and Madhya Pradesh's Decoreer turns terracotta into turtles, urlis and sculptural lamps.

The luxury hamper end of the market

At the top end, hotels and design houses are treating the hamper itself as the craft object. Robb Report India's Diwali gifting edit leads with The Leela Palace New Delhi's Signatures collection, built around a special-edition Pichwai artwork by master artist Rajaram Sharma of Nathdwara; its Opulence Hamper, priced at Rs 18,500 plus taxes, pairs artisanal mithai or baklava with chocolate rocks, macarons, tea and Ganesha and Lakshmi idols. Savorworks' Sensory Trunk (Rs 20,000) packs artisan chocolates, specialty coffee and aromatics-matched candles into a handcrafted leatherette trunk, while Conrad Bengaluru's Heart of Delight (Rs 50,000) combines handcrafted sweets, wine, body care and spa experiences.

How to choose

The pattern across both edits is the same: a gift that keeps being used after Diwali night — a diya set that returns each year, tableware that hosts the next family dinner — beats a consumable that is gone in a week. For diaspora readers sending gifts home, the studio labels are the practical route: most take online orders, several offer corporate customisation and split delivery, and the craft story travels with the gift. Order ahead of the festival rush, and check delivery windows before Dhanteras.
